input.question: How are telecommunications possible in outer space if there is no medium (atmosphere) for the waves to traverse?
input.ground_truth: The discovery that electromagnetic waves don't require a medium to travel through is one of the more important ones in the history of science. The idea of the aether was disproved by the famous Michelson-Morley experiment. Visible light, radio waves, microwaves etc are all electromagnetic waves of different frequencies, and there is no issue with the travelling through space. In fact, the presence of the atmosphere can serve to hinder them, as it scatters higher frequency waves.

Okay! Imagine you want to talk to your friend who is far, far away—so far that there’s nothing but empty space between you, not even air.

On Earth, when you talk or use a walkie-talkie, your voice or the radio waves travel through the air. That’s called a “medium.” But in space, there is no air, no water, no anything—just empty space.

But here’s a cool thing: some kinds of waves don’t need air or anything to travel! They are called “electromagnetic waves.” Light is one of them, and radio waves (which carry your phone calls and TV shows) are another.

These waves can travel through empty space all by themselves! So, when astronauts talk to Earth, they use special radios that send out these waves. They zoom through the empty space super fast and reach big antennas on Earth.

So, even without air, we can still talk to each other in space using these special waves!
